siftei_kohen.en:
The purchaser swears in accordance with the enactment of the Sages. Since the produce has already left the seller's possession and lies in the public domain, the purchaser swears and takes it. Had it been in the purchaser's possession, he would take only a hesset oath and retain it. Had it remained in the shopkeeper's possession, the shopkeeper would take a hesset oath and retain it.
“And you carried them into your house.” Maimonides explains that if the shopkeeper says, “I never sold you these fruits lying in the public domain,” the shopkeeper takes a stringent oath that this is so and the fruits are returned to him, since he never admitted selling them. If they were in his shop, he would take only a hesset oath. Bartenura writes likewise, and this is also the view of the Rif, as the Ran reports from the Rif's Arabic commentary, and of Baal HaTerumot. Because the early authorities offer five different explanations of this Mishna and none appears satisfactory, I will set out the interpretation that appears to me correct. The Mishna states: A buyer tells a shopkeeper, “Give me produce for a dinar.” The shopkeeper gives it to him and then asks for the dinar. The buyer says, “I already gave it to you and you placed it in your purse.” The buyer swears. If the buyer gave the dinar and then asked for the produce, and the shopkeeper said, “I already gave it to you and you carried it into your house,” the shopkeeper swears. Rabbi Yehuda says that whoever holds the produce has the stronger position. The parallel rule is stated regarding a money changer. The Gemara adds that Rabbi Yehuda's qualification applies when the produce is piled between them and both dispute it, but once the buyer has slung it behind him, the burden of proof rests on the claimant. The Rif and Maimonides understand the case as produce lying in the public domain, with the distinction that in one clause the shopkeeper admits the sale and in the other he denies it. Several difficulties arise. The wording “he gave it to him” ordinarily means an actual delivery. Rabbi Yehuda's phrase “whoever holds the produce” also implies actual possession. The Mishna gives no hint that the shopkeeper admits the sale in one clause and denies it in the other. Nor is “he slung it behind him” a natural expression for bringing it fully into his domain. The Tur, following Rabbenu Tam and the Rosh, explains that the shopkeeper measured the produce into the buyer's vessels while they were still in the shopkeeper's domain. In the reverse clause the buyer placed the dinar in the shop before the shopkeeper took it. Because each item has partly left the prior possessor's control, the party seeking to retain it swears and collects. Rabbi Yehuda holds that an ordinary shopkeeper does not measure produce before receiving payment. This explanation also remains difficult, because “he gave it to him” sounds like an actual transfer, and Rabbi Yehuda should have stated directly that a shopkeeper does not extend credit. It is also difficult to understand why the Sages would disagree if this particular shopkeeper was known not to sell on credit. Rashi understands the Mishna literally. In the first clause the produce is already behind the buyer, while the dinar remains with him. Rabbi Yehuda says that the buyer need not swear because a shopkeeper who does not sell on credit would not have released the produce without payment. In the second clause Rabbi Yehuda agrees that the shopkeeper swears, because the produce remains in the shopkeeper's domain. This explanation is more direct, but it is still difficult that Rabbi Yehuda's statement appears after both clauses and is expressed generally. The Raavad explains that in the first clause the produce is in the buyer's basket behind him, but the dispute arose before he left the shop. The Sages therefore imposed an oath. In the second clause the produce is piled on the ground. Rabbi Yehuda says that only while the produce is piled between them is there an oath enactment, whereas once it is behind the buyer the burden of proof is on the claimant. This too requires forcing Rabbi Yehuda's qualification partly onto one clause and partly onto another. The Semag, following Rabbenu Chananel, explains that the produce is in the public domain, or that both parties grasp the dinar. Yet it is difficult why the shopkeeper should have a stronger right to swear and take than the buyer. The correct explanation appears to me as follows. This Mishna continues the category of those who swear and collect. Just as the shopkeeper on his ledger and the workers swear and collect although the employer has only an uncertain claim against them, so too here the dispute itself is uncertain on one side. In the first clause it is agreed that the shopkeeper gave the produce, which is already in the buyer's basket behind him. The shopkeeper, not seeing the dinar before him, thinks it was not paid. The buyer says that he paid it before receiving the produce and that the shopkeeper placed it in his purse but forgot because he was occupied measuring the produce. Although the shopkeeper's claim is only uncertain and the produce is in the buyer's basket, the dispute arose while they were still in the shop before the buyer brought it home. The Sages therefore treat the buyer as one who is still collecting from the shop and require a Mishnaic oath. In the second clause it is agreed that the buyer gave the dinar and it remains in the shopkeeper's hand. The buyer, accustomed to carrying produce home in several loads, thinks he has not yet received it. The shopkeeper says that he gave the produce before receiving the dinar and that the buyer carried it home but forgot. Although the buyer's claim is only uncertain, and the dinar and produce are both effectively in the shopkeeper's control, the dispute arose before the shopkeeper placed the dinar in his purse. The Sages therefore treat him as one who is now collecting from the buyer and require him to swear. Rabbi Yehuda disputes both clauses. In his view, whoever presently holds the produce is treated as though he already brought it home, even if the dispute arose in the shop. Only where the produce is piled between them, equally accessible to both, must the party making the definite claim swear before taking it. This explains the baraita's word “when,” which here introduces a limitation and dispute. Rabbi Yehuda does not say that a shopkeeper never extends credit, because he agrees that a shopkeeper may do so. His rule rests on possession. A money changer is different, because a money changer ordinarily does not hand over coins before receiving the dinar. Therefore, even when the money is in the money changer's hand, his claim that he gave change before receiving the dinar is inherently implausible. This reading also explains the Gemara's discussion of why both a shopkeeper and a money changer had to be taught. Produce spoils, so one might have thought the Sages require an oath only there because shopkeepers commonly release produce before receiving payment, whereas coins do not spoil. Conversely, one might have thought Rabbi Yehuda's rule applies only to money changing. The Yerushalmi and Tosefta strongly support this explanation. They state that Rabbi Yehuda spoke in dispute, not merely in explanation, and that when the basket lies between them he agrees with the Sages, whereas when it has left the control of either party the burden of proof lies on the claimant. Their language shows that Rabbi Yehuda's rule applies whichever party presently holds the item. This contradicts the readings of the Rif, Maimonides, Rabbenu Tam, Rashi, the Raavad, and the Semag in their respective details, but it accords with the plain sense of the Mishna, Tosefta, Yerushalmi, and Bavli. Nevertheless, when the produce is entirely in the shopkeeper's domain and both are uncertain whether the dinar was paid, the Sages agree that the buyer cannot swear and take. This is the ordinary case of one who says, “You owe me one hundred,” and the other says, “I do not know,” where the possessor is exempt. Likewise, if the dinar is entirely in the buyer's possession and the shopkeeper claims definitely that produce was delivered while the buyer is uncertain, the shopkeeper does not swear and take. At most, because of Rav Nachman's enactment, the possessor takes a hesset oath that he does not know. There is also reason to distinguish between a dispute that comes before beit din while the produce is still behind the buyer or the dinar still in the shopkeeper's hand, and one in which the item was already carried fully home or placed in the purse before litigation. Rabbi Yehuda certainly exempts once the item has been brought home. It is therefore preferable to say that the Sages disagree only while the parties come before us with the item still in the intermediate state. Moreover, their oath is an enactment, and one should not extend an enactment beyond its stated case. Accordingly, once the buyer has brought the produce home, he is exempt without a Mishnaic oath. If the shopkeeper makes a definite claim, the buyer takes only a hesset oath. The same applies when the shopkeeper has already placed the dinar in his purse. As for produce lying in the public domain where both parties make definite claims, the Rif and Maimonides derived their ruling from their interpretation of the Mishna. Once that interpretation is rejected, the independent law requires analysis. At first glance one might apply the rule that the stronger party prevails, as where neither party possesses a disputed boat. Yet when there is a prior owner, the property remains with that prior owner even if presently in a neutral place. We rule against Sumchus that property standing in a meadow remains with the prior owner, and the same applies in the public domain. Thus the produce remains presumptively the shopkeeper's, and he takes it after a hesset oath. Even if the shopkeeper is uncertain and the buyer is certain, prior ownership ordinarily prevails. In practice, however, this remains difficult because Maimonides rules differently in a related case where both parties are uncertain. Where the shopkeeper measured the produce into the buyer's vessel while it remains in the shopkeeper's domain, the result depends on whether the shopkeeper said, “Acquire through this vessel.” If he did, the buyer's vessel acquired the produce for him, and he is treated as possessor. He therefore takes the produce after a Mishnaic oath, whether the shopkeeper's denial is definite or uncertain. If the shopkeeper did not authorize acquisition through the vessel, the buyer's vessel in the seller's domain does not acquire according to the Rif and Maimonides, and even according to the Rosh the issue is unresolved. The produce therefore remains with the prior owner, the shopkeeper, who is exempt after a hesset oath. If there are no witnesses whether the shopkeeper said, “Acquire through this vessel,” and the buyer claims that he did while the shopkeeper denies it, one might attempt to treat the buyer as possessor through a double doubt. Yet monetary law generally follows possession rather than a double doubt. Since the shopkeeper is the prior owner, it is more reasonable to leave the produce with him. Even if the shopkeeper admits authorizing the acquisition, he may perhaps be believed to say that payment was not made by virtue of a migo that he could have denied authorizing acquisition altogether. This point requires study. If the shopkeeper is uncertain about payment and admits that he authorized acquisition, the buyer is certainly the possessor and swears and takes. If both parties are uncertain, and the produce lies in the buyer's vessel in the shopkeeper's domain without authorization to acquire, it remains with the shopkeeper as prior owner. This differs from ordinary jointly held property where neither side has prior ownership, in which case parties who are both uncertain divide without an oath. The rules attributed to Rabbenu Tam and the Rosh may be reconciled with these conclusions by saying that they discuss a case where the shopkeeper expressly authorized the buyer's vessel to acquire. The first and second clauses would then be parallel, each involving property already in the other party's acquiring domain. Regarding the Semag's case where both grasp the dinar, or where it lies in the public domain, his conclusion that the shopkeeper swears and takes is not convincing. If both grasp it, they divide it under the rules of two people holding a garment, with the required oath. If it lies in the public domain and neither has possession, the stronger party prevails, unless prior ownership can properly be applied. All of this is stated as law for study, not as a practical ruling against the great early authorities. The interpretation of the Mishna and baraita themselves, however, appears correct for both law and practice, since no authority states a rule contradicting it. May Hashem show us wonders from His Torah and save me from error. Cited cross-references in the source include: 3, 40, 50, 63, 80, 81, 90, 100, 120, 200, 220, 486, 520.

urim_vetumim_tumim.he: אמר לחנוני וכו' רבו בזה הפי' והש"ך האריך להשיג ולהקשות על כל הפי' ובאמת כל קושיתו אין בהם כדאי שצריך להשיג עליהם כי כל דקדוקו הם דקדוק עניות וח"ו לדייק כולי האי לדחות דברי קדמונים ואולי דייקת כולי האי ממש לא תנאי ולא מצינו הלכה ברורה בש"ס. ואולם כי חשב לפרש פי' אחר ועינה מלבו וכבר עמד הגאון חכם צבי ז"ל בהגהתו לט"ז והקשה עליו קושי' חזקה עד שנדחה פי' ואין ראוי לאומרו כלל. ע"ש ואין לנו שיור בזה רק לישב קושית הש"ך על סמ"ג דסמ"ג פי' ודעתו כשהפירו' מונחים בר"ה והחנוני תובע המעות והבעה"ב טוען פרעתיך כבר ישבע הלוקח בנק"ח ויטול פירות וכשהפירות ברשות חנוני ודינר בר"ה וחנוני טוען כבר נתתי עבורו פירות והלוקח טוען לא כי עדיין לא קבלתי פירות ישבע החנוני ועל זה הקשה הש"ך מ"ש מרישא ולמה בזה יד חנוני יותר יפה מיד לוקח עד שישבע ויטול. ונראה דלק"מ דבכל מקום רואין על מה הטענה כשהפירות מונחים בר"ה שניהם מודים דפירות הללו הם מונחים לכדי שיטלם הלוקח ואין כאן טענה על הפירות ובפרט לפי מה שכתב המ"מ דהגביהן הלוקח וקנאם בדרכי קנין וא"כ כל התביעה רק בדמי מעות והרי זה כתביעה בפ"ע וכל התביעה רק על המעות א"כ הלוקח נשבע ונפטר וכמו כן שהדינר בר"ה ולא נחלקו כלל על הדינר שראוי ליתן לו לחנוני רק כל הפלפול כי לוקח תובע פירות וזה אומר כבר נתתי פירות ואם כן הסכסוך בפירות החנוני מוחזק והממע"ה ולק"מ. אמנם סמיכת הש"ך בדברי ירושלמי דקתני באם יוצא מתחת יד אחד מהן עדיין היא במחלוקת ומזה מבואר דאפילו תחת יד הלוקח מ"מ נחלקו ת"ק ור' יהודא זהו דלא כפי' הרי"ף ותוס' וסייעתם דסבירא להו אם הוא ת"י אחד א"צ כלל שבועה וזהו מהטענה באמת אלא שאף שאין ראיה כלל מירושלמי כי הגהה והגי' משונה כנודע אף גם כאשר עיינתי בירושלמי מצאתי ראיתי שכתב כך על משנה אר"ח במחלוקת אר' יהוד' אימתי בזמן שהקופה מונחת בין שניהם אבל אם היא יוצאה מת"י א' מהן עוד היא במחלוקת עכ"ל ולפי' הש"ך פי' מחלוקת היינו הך ר' יהוד' ורבנן וזהו אינו מסדר הלשון שיהיה ר' יהודה אומר על עצמו עוד היא מחלוקת ויהיה מכוון שהוא פליג והל"ל ביוצא מתחת יד אחד מהן חכמים אומרים כך ואני אומר כך ומה שאמר ר"ח מתחילה במחלוקת אין לו מובן כלל דאם נתכוון דפליגי חכמים ור"י מה קמ"ל הא משנה לפניך דפליגי חכמים ור"י ואם כוונתו לומר שאפי' יוצא מתחת יד אחד מהן ג"כ פליגי זהו לא נזכר כלל בדבריו ועיקר חסר ולכן נראה דידוע בכל הש"ס במקום הספק לב"ד ס"ל לחכמים הממע"ה וסומכוס יחלוקו ואם כן קאמר ר"ח הא דתנן במשנה דישבע חנוני ויטול או בעה"ב כמבואר במשנה זהו הכל לחכמים דס"ל דהממע"ה ולכך מי שהוא יותר מוחזק נוטל רק מכל מקום החמירו עליו שישבע שבועת נק"ח אבל לסומכוס דסבירא ליה בעלמא יחלוקו אף כאן אין זה שחזקתו יותר משל חבירו נוטל הכל רק יחלוקו וזהו כוונתו במחלוקת ור"י פליג וסבירא ליה דאם בר"ה הרי זה ודאי בחזקת מרא קמא ואין כאן ספק לב"ד רק ביוצא מת"י השני בזו במחלוקת דחכמים סבירא להו לעולם הממע"ה וסומכוס ס"ל הואיל יש לשני יד בו הוי ליה דדרא דממון ויחלוקו לסומכוס וזהו מאמרו עוד היא במחלוקת היינו מחלוקת הידוע בש"ס בכל דוכתא והבקי בלשון ירושלמי תלמודו בלשנא קלילי דנקט יראה שנוטים הדברים אל מרכז האמת ודבריו כך הם עניים במקום הזה ועשירים במקום אחר:
urim_vetumim_tumim.en: If he said to the shopkeeper, etc. Many explanations have been offered, and the Shach argues at length against all of them. In truth, his objections are not strong enough to justify rejecting the earlier authorities. They depend on excessively fine textual deductions, and if one insisted on such precision everywhere, hardly a tannaitic formulation or clear Talmudic law would survive. The Shach then proposes an explanation of his own, but the gaon Chacham Tzvi, in his glosses to the Taz, raises a powerful objection that refutes it entirely. See there. We therefore need only answer the Shach’s objection to the Semag. The Semag explains that when the produce is lying in the public domain, the shopkeeper demands the money and the purchaser says, “I already paid you,” the purchaser swears while holding a sacred object and takes the produce. When the produce remains in the shopkeeper’s possession and the dinar lies in the public domain, while the shopkeeper says, “I already gave you produce for it,” and the purchaser says, “No, I have not yet received the produce,” the shopkeeper swears. The Shach asks why the shopkeeper’s position is stronger in the latter case than the purchaser’s in the former, such that the shopkeeper may swear and retain. There is no difficulty. In every case we identify the actual subject of the dispute. When the produce lies in the public domain, both parties agree that this produce is there for the purchaser to take. There is no dispute concerning ownership of the produce. This is especially clear according to the Maggid Mishneh, who says that the purchaser already lifted the produce and acquired it through an effective kinyan. The only dispute is whether the purchase money was paid, which is an independent monetary claim. The purchaser therefore swears and is exempt from paying again. Conversely, when the dinar lies in the public domain, the parties do not dispute that this dinar is to go to the shopkeeper. Their dispute concerns the produce: the purchaser demands produce, while the shopkeeper says, “I already gave it to you.” The disputed subject is therefore produce in the shopkeeper’s possession, and the rule is that one who seeks to extract from a possessor bears the burden of proof. Thus the shopkeeper swears and retains. The Shach also relies on the Yerushalmi, which says that when the object emerges from the possession of one of them, “it remains in dispute,” and he infers that even when the object is actually under the purchaser’s control, the first tanna and Rabbi Yehudah still disagree. This conflicts with the Rif, Tosafot, and their followers, who hold that when the object is in the possession of one party no oath is needed at all. But there is no reliable proof from the Yerushalmi. Its text and emendation are notoriously difficult. Moreover, on examining the Yerushalmi, I found the passage reads: Rabbi Chiya says, “It is in dispute.” Rabbi Yehudah says, “When is this? When the basket lies between them. But if it comes out from under the hand of one of them, it is still in dispute.” According to the Shach, “in dispute” would mean the dispute between Rabbi Yehudah and the Sages. This does not fit the language. It would be strange for Rabbi Yehudah to say of his own ruling, “it is still in dispute,” meaning that he himself disagrees. He should have said directly, “If it comes out from under one party, the Sages say such-and-such and I say otherwise.” Nor is Rabbi Chiya’s opening statement, “It is in dispute,” intelligible if he merely means that the Mishnah itself records a dispute between Rabbi Yehudah and the Sages. That teaches nothing. And if he means that they dispute even when the object is under one party’s control, that crucial point is absent from his statement. The better explanation is based on a familiar dispute throughout the Talmud. Where property is in doubt, the Sages hold that the claimant must bring proof, while Sumchus says they divide. Rabbi Chiya is saying that the Mishnah’s rule that either the shopkeeper or the employer swears and takes follows the Sages, who give the property to the stronger possessor, though here they additionally require that possessor to take an oath while holding a sacred object. According to Sumchus, by contrast, the fact that one party has the stronger possession does not give him the entire property; they divide. That is the “dispute” Rabbi Chiya references. Rabbi Yehudah then qualifies the matter: when the basket lies in the public domain, he regards it as certainly remaining in the chazakah of its original owner, so there is no true doubt before beit din. But if it actually comes out from under the hand of the other party, then the familiar dispute remains. The Sages still say that the claimant must bring proof, whereas Sumchus says that since the other party has some possession in it, it is a genuine contested fund and they divide. Thus “it is still in dispute” refers to the well-known Sages and Sumchus dispute found throughout the Talmud, not to Rabbi Yehudah disputing himself. Anyone familiar with the concise idiom of the Yerushalmi will see that this reading approaches the truth. Its words are poor in one place and rich in another.

urim_vetumim_urim.he:
הלוקח נשבע כיון שחנוני מודה שהפירות הם ראוים ליתנם ללוקח ובשביל זה מונחים בר"ה שקנאם הלוקח רק תובע מעות עבורם ולכך הבעה"ב שהוא לוקח נשבע והואיל ונוטל הפירות נשבע בנק"ח:
והולכתם וכו' ופירות הללו מעולם לא מכרתים לך א"כ אלו היה מונחים ברשות חנוני היה נאמן בהיס' רק הואיל שמונחים בר"ה צריך שבועה וע"ת מ"ש בזה ע"ש:
urim_vetumim_urim.en:
The psalmist swore that the fruit they would see for them to take away, and for this reason, they would only take care of them, and that it would take them to swear, and that the fruit was sworn in:
And I brought them, etc. The shopkeeper says, 'I never sold you these particular fruits.' Had the fruits still been in his own domain, he would be believed with hesset. Because they are now lying in the public domain, he must take the stronger oath described here. See Tumim.
